messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Priya is a thirty-year-old South Asian woman who works as a software engineer and has been married for three years. She presented for therapy after her PCL-5 score of 46 suggested clinically significant post-traumatic stress, though she herself described her reasons for coming in with characteristic understatement: she said only that she had not been sleeping and that things at home were "getting harder to manage." What emerged across the first several sessions was a childhood defined by her father's intermittent but severe physical violence — episodes that typically began in the evenings, when the smell of alcohol on his breath signalled what was coming, and that ended with Priya hiding in a corner of the kitchen, her cheek pressed against the cold tile, the taste of blood pooling at the back of her throat. These were the textures of her most formative years, and they had never fully receded.

Priya is now thirty, professionally accomplished, and living in what she describes as a safe and loving marriage. None of that has quieted what her body continues to register as danger. The smell of alcohol — at a colleague's birthday gathering, at a dinner party, even in the hand sanitiser her office keeps at the entrance — lands in her chest before it reaches her conscious mind. In those moments, she feels her heart rate climb and her jaw tighten, and she finds herself scanning the room for exits. The smell of sweat, too — on a crowded train, in a gym locker room — carries the same charge, as does a particular metallic-sweet taste she occasionally encounters and cannot fully name. Each of these sensory cues functions as an immediate threat signal, pulling her nervous system into a state of high alert that she cannot talk herself out of. She checks the locks on the front door before bed, sometimes twice, sometimes more; she lies awake long after her husband has fallen asleep, listening for sounds she cannot identify. Even in the stillness of her own home, she has come to believe that relaxation is a kind of recklessness — that the moment she lets her guard down is precisely the moment something will happen.

The memories themselves are not clean or linear. Priya cannot reconstruct the events of her childhood in any stable sequence; she knows certain things happened, but the order shifts, and details that should be central seem to dissolve when she reaches for them. More distressing still is what happens when the memories do surface: they arrive with a force that feels less like recollection than re-immersion, and the emotional overwhelm is so immediate that she finds herself pushing the images away before they can fully form. This blocking, which feels to her like self-protection, means she has never been able to sit with any single memory long enough to understand it. The fragmented, unresolved quality of these recollections keeps her nervous system primed — because what cannot be processed cannot be filed away as past, and so the threat they carry remains perpetually present. When a memory fragment surfaces during a sleepless night, it does not feel like remembering; it feels like warning.

The relationship between her memory and her triggers runs in both directions, and this is what has made the past year particularly difficult. A sensory cue — the smell of alcohol at a work event — will pull a fragment of memory forward, incomplete and overwhelming, which in turn heightens her sense that danger is near, which then makes her more vigilant to the next sensory cue. Over months, this has narrowed her world in ways that have become impossible to ignore. She has begun declining after-work social events, citing workload, and her manager has noticed her increasing withdrawal from team activities. Her husband, patient but worried, has remarked that she seems to be somewhere else even when she is sitting beside him.

What finally brought Priya to seek help was a moment at a restaurant three months ago, when a dish arrived carrying a taste she recognised, and she had to leave the table and sit alone in the bathroom for twenty minutes, shaking. She told no one what had happened. She is most afraid, she says, that this will never get better — and most hoping, quietly, that someone will finally be able to help her understand what she is actually remembering.
